title: How AI and EdTech Are Changing Further and Higher Education
label: 10 November 2026 · AI and EdTech in Education
summary: Further and higher education leaders, staff representatives and students’ union officers told the Committee that AI and educational technology are already reshaping teaching, assessment, workload and access. They welcomed opportunities—simulations, personalised support, administrative automation—but warned about rising workload, inconsistent governance, widening digital inequality, unclear assessment rules and variable staff training. Witnesses urged principled national guidance, investment in infrastructure and staff development, stronger guardrails on data and judged, human-led assessment reforms.

chapters.title: Big picture: opportunities and worries
chapters.takeaway: AI is being used across colleges and universities for teaching, admin and support, offering big gains but creating real risks on workload, equity and governance.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We want to hear how AI and edtech are changing further and higher education and how institutions should prepare students for an AI-rich future.

turns.speaker: Cath Sezen
turns.text: It's early days, but colleges are keen: staff use AI to plan lessons and support students, and specialist 'digiTEC' colleges focus on digital and AI skills.

turns.speaker: Chris Loveday
turns.text: AI helps teaching, admin and operations. It can reduce workload if used well, but staff and students need training and safeguards on misinfo, bias and data use.

turns.speaker: Mary Meekings
turns.text: UCU members' experiences vary widely—some embrace AI, some worry. Staff are teaching themselves and sometimes paying for tools; that can't be sustainable.

turns.speaker: Ben Rowland
turns.text: Providers report fastest gains in back-office automation, then teaching prep; learning and assessment improvements lag. Small, practical providers experiment quickly with supplier help.

chapters.title: Curriculum, skills and digital fairness
chapters.takeaway: Everyone will need basic digital and critical-thinking skills, but colleges fear the digital divide will leave many behind without proper devices, connectivity and training.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: How will AI affect new post-16 reforms like V-levels and T-levels?

turns.speaker: Cath Sezen
turns.text: Digital content is being added to T-levels and V-levels, but qualifications move slowly; we must speed that up while keeping higher technical pathways available.

turns.speaker: Ben Rowland
turns.text: Simulation and VR now make realistic practice affordable—useful for vocational training and for building confidence in maths and English resits.

turns.speaker: Chris Loveday
turns.text: Curriculum must teach how to use AI, and institutions must protect students who lack devices, internet or paid-model access—there are four equity pillars to cover.

turns.speaker: Mary Meekings
turns.text: We risk a digital underclass or, conversely, students relying too much on machines. The human relationship in education must be preserved.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Could AI help reduce the number of young people who are NEET?

turns.speaker: Ben Rowland
turns.text: AI can support outreach and retraining, but social factors and employer engagement matter; apprenticeships—including older workers—are crucial routes in.

turns.speaker: Chris Loveday
turns.text: Using live data to identify at-risk students earlier helps target support and prevent disengagement; tech should guide strategy, not replace it.

chapters.title: Assessment, integrity and what we measure
chapters.takeaway: AI forces a rethink of assessment: practical, in-person checks, or AI-aware tasks, plus oral or process-based evidence, will be needed to certify learning.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: How should assessment change now that students can use generative AI?

turns.speaker: Chris Loveday
turns.text: We should reassess softer skills like critical thinking and presentations and use timed, supervised tasks where appropriate; marking tells you about students too.

turns.speaker: Cath Sezen
turns.text: Vocational assessment should focus on doing the task, not just written recall. This moment may justify a wider rethink of assessment design.

turns.speaker: Ben Rowland
turns.text: Surveys show assessment is the area least affected so far. Awarding bodies want to innovate but feel regulators like Ofqual are not aligned with frontline needs.

turns.speaker: Manuela Perteghella
turns.text: Are dissertations and postgraduate research at risk from AI?

turns.speaker: Professor Simon Banks
turns.text: Research and dissertations can still include oral defences and ongoing supervision; the discipline and how central writing or coding are will determine risk.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Armstrong
turns.text: Students report mixed effects: many use AI to summarise or plan rather than to submit unedited essays, but some feel guilty and worry they are learning less.

turns.speaker: Michael Webb
turns.text: Technical approaches include supervised assessments, process monitoring that records how work was produced, and oral checks—no single fix will work as tools evolve.

chapters.title: Staffing, workload and governance
chapters.takeaway: AI can reduce tedious tasks but currently often shifts workload into checking and adjusting outputs; colleges lack consistent governance and need funded training.

turns.speaker: Jodie Gosling
turns.text: Will AI cut staff numbers or just change staff skills?

turns.speaker: Charlotte Armstrong
turns.text: Staff will need time for training. The best evidence shows AI plus human feedback works well—losing staff-student interaction would harm quality.

turns.speaker: Professor Simon Banks
turns.text: I expect upskilling rather than mass reductions. Many staff use AI to do new things, and time saved often gets reinvested into teaching in different ways.

turns.speaker: Chris Loveday
turns.text: Governance is the biggest risk. Many colleges lack clear AI policies, data protection officers or guidance, so staff may accidentally share sensitive data with free tools.

turns.speaker: Ben Rowland
turns.text: Larger providers have governance driven by scale or private owners; small providers struggle. Claiming extra learner-support funds is also administratively hard.

turns.speaker: Mary Meekings
turns.text: Workload surveys show workloads rising year-on-year. AI hasn't yet produced a clear sector-wide workload reduction—teachers need time, training and guardrails.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: Who should decide if a product is safe: suppliers, colleges or government?

turns.speaker: Chris Loveday
turns.text: Suppliers sell products and will lock customers in. Responsibility primarily sits with institutions, but colleges need sector-level guidance and support.

turns.speaker: Cath Sezen
turns.text: Colleges want road maps and baseline guidance. We should agree guardrails and avoid multiple bodies duplicating guidance—coordination between Jisc, Ufi and sector bodies helps.

chapters.title: Higher education: research, equity and a national framework
chapters.takeaway: Universities are already experimenting; research gains look promising, but students and staff face uneven support—principles-led national guidance and funding for training are needed.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Turning to higher education—how is student AI use affecting deep learning and critical thinking?

turns.speaker: Lewis Wilson
turns.text: Students use AI for many reasons, including lack of staff time. It doesn't always mean they learn less, but shortcuts risk long-term skills erosion if used in place of study.

turns.speaker: Professor Simon Banks
turns.text: Impact varies by student and by support. With training, AI can amplify learning; without it, students may 'offload' vital cognitive work.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Armstrong
turns.text: HEPI surveys show about half of students say AI improves their experience, 16% say it worsens it; those who feel worse often worry they are learning less despite getting grades.

turns.speaker: Peter Swallow
turns.text: Are universities equipping students with the AI and critical-literacy skills employers want?

turns.speaker: Michael Webb
turns.text: Universities want to prepare students, but delivery varies. Infrastructure, funding and staff capacity affect how well lessons reach students.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Armstrong
turns.text: Students in arts and humanities feel less well equipped than STEM students; discipline and institution make a big difference.

turns.speaker: Professor Simon Banks
turns.text: Universities must embed AI skills in disciplines while keeping core knowledge and transferable skills—communication, judgement and teamwork—at the heart of degrees.

turns.speaker: Darren Paffey
turns.text: Should there be a national framework for AI use in universities?

turns.speaker: Michael Webb
turns.text: Universities need autonomy; a rigid national rule would either be too vague or too prescriptive. Sector-level principles and guidance work better.

turns.speaker: Charlotte Armstrong
turns.text: Yes to guidance on values and principles rather than hard rules—something like Ireland's higher-education authority approach, not central diktat.

turns.speaker: Lewis Wilson
turns.text: Any framework must be resourced properly so institutions can implement it and no students are left behind.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send any further evidence or detail to the Committee—your points on governance, assessment redesign and funding were especially helpful.
